body:
"Obtained from untrusted sources are stored outside the web root and limited permissions." -> "Untrusted file data obtained from untrusted sources are stored outside the web root and limited permissions"

16.3 Adding the need for AV I think is excessive as using a mime-aware library such as Apache Tika should largely remove the need for AV unless you allow users to upload dangerous file types such as EXEs or files that support active content (PDFs, Office documents, etc.)

There is no mention of the following controls:

- size limits + number of files uploaded limits
- quota limits per user (if needed)
- possibly using a different sub-domain to serve user uploads to prevent XSS
- the uploading of in-intentionally uploading executable code such as SVG images which are then served directly back to users

comments.body:
I think that adding an item explicitly related to more thorough file type verification might be useful.  16.3 and 16.4 kind of touch on it but I think that we might want to emphasize two parts:

- not relying simply on file extensions and content-type sent (libmagic is useful).  
- verifying that the web server is configured correctly to not serve dynamic content (refer to the recent jQuery Plugin vuln (https://zd.net/2CUnToG) as an example)

The first won't completely remove issues such as polyglot attacks but when combined with the 2nd, should provide adequate protection
I wonder if we need to look at the whole supply-chain issue here?

Why did 16.4 get changed from 

> [...] to prevent remote/local file inclusion vulnerabilities.
to
> [...] to prevent remote/local code execution vulnerabilities.

This seems like a wholly different thing, where both of them are relevant. Wouldn't it make sense to have both of them as separate points?
This is a duplicate, closing and moving to #377
